title: MekongPhon: A Large-Scale Parallel IPA Corpus for Lao and Khmer
scope: Paper reports 1,314,779 Khmer orthography–IPA sentence pairs; seed lexicon 8,026 word–IPA entries derived from Headley (1977), with a two-author 500-entry review (99.2% sample accuracy; reviewers are proficient L2 speakers, not native speakers). Pinned repository snapshot f80f6c1840c4818b51e05f2e00cded4701a5b662 contains 8,040 rows in data/lexicons/khmer_lexicon.csv: 8,026 word entries plus 10 Khmer digits and 4 punctuation tokens. data/splits/khmer_train.csv (7,940) and khmer_eval.csv (100) partition those 8,040 lexicon rows; data/sampled/khmer_500.csv is a 500-row word-level subset, not a sentence sample. The generated 1.3m sentence-pair corpus is not present in the repository. The OPUS download script names NLLB-v1, ParaCrawl-Bonus-v9 and OpenSubtitles-v2024; the sentence labels are generated by longest-match trie lookup over the word lexicon, not independent sentence transcription. The repository has no root LICENSE and GitHub reports license=null. pipeline/convert_khmer.py imports absent dict_transliterator and clean modules and points to absent data paths; pipeline/split_lexicon.py has the Khmer split call commented out. The README's sentence-split/sample descriptions do not match the committed word-level files. This remains a secondary model/lexical comparator only, not blind adjudicated IPA gold; the reported <2% CER is under the paper's dictionary-seeded setup, not independent human-IPA accuracy. The scraper does not retain or validate the SEALang entry source identifier; the committed lexicon has no per-item source locators.
provenance: The paper identifies Headley (1977) as the Khmer dictionary source and SEALang as the host. pipeline/scrape.py sends source=headley77 in the query but parse_sealang_html_file_khmer returns the first <entry> and serializes only orth/prontarget; it does not persist a per-row source identifier or validate the returned entry's source ID. The 8,040-row CSV has no per-item citations. pipeline/README.md says numerals and punctuation were manually added. The published methodology says the seed lexicon was reviewed by two authors on a 500-entry random sample, but it does not report inter-annotator agreement or a double-blind independent adjudication protocol.
profile: Philip N. Jenner's 1979 review of Headley (1977), DOI 10.15144/PL-C49.431, quotes the dictionary's stated pronunciation target as 'Standard Khmer as spoken by educated persons throughout the Khmer-speaking area' (p. 432), not specifically contemporary Phnom Penh. Jenner notes that main entries may include alternate pronunciations and that the dictionary is based on the 1967/68 Buddhist Institute dictionary with secondary sources. A separate bibliographic description notes current literary/standard spoken forms as well as obsolete, dialectal and archaic forms. Therefore the lexicon cannot be assumed to represent one homogeneous modern Phnom Penh careful-citation profile.
quality_review: The paper reports 4/500 Khmer seed entries inaccurate (99.2% sample accuracy). It says both reviewers are highly proficient second-language speakers rather than native speakers. This is a two-author sample review, not a reported inter-annotator agreement coefficient, full-lexicon audit, native-speaker adjudication, or independent project gold.
license: Dataset license/redistribution rights UNKNOWN. The LREC proceedings CC BY-NC 4.0 applies to the paper, not automatically to the dataset; the Hugging Face model's Apache-2.0 label applies to model artifacts, not training data. The paper cites a generic SEAlang 'Creative Commons open license' without a version. SHACHI metadata for the broader SEAlang Khmer dictionary identifies source materials as copyrighted, including Headley (1977); MekongPhon's scraper specifically requests source=headley77, so rights for that exact source must be confirmed rather than inferred from the generic SEAlang statement. OPUS inputs have distinct terms: NLLB-v1 ODC-By with original-source terms; ParaCrawl-Bonus-v9 CC0 for the package but its LICENSE says providers do not own underlying text; OpenSubtitles-v2024 LICENSE disclaims ownership of underlying text. The concatenation/sort pipeline drops per-row source provenance. Obtain explicit dataset-specific permission and item-level source/rights manifests before redistribution or gold import.
limitations: Candidate historical-dictionary IPA reference and source-attested diagnostic only, not independent gold. Exact profile is not specified and Headley includes a range of current, dialectal, obsolete and archaic material. No per-entry source locators are present; the scraper does not persist/validate entry source IDs. The 500-item review is small and performed by two L2 reviewers; no IAA or independent native-speaker adjudication is reported. The published test uses a 100-entry seed-lexicon holdout and OPUS sentences generated through the same dictionary mapping, with exact train-sentence overlap removed; this is dictionary-seeded unseen-lexeme evaluation, not independent speech transcription. The checked-in split script writes *_cleaned.csv filenames while committed files are khmer_train.csv/khmer_eval.csv; convert_khmer.py references ../data/khmer_train.csv and ../data/khmer_ipa.csv, neither present in the pinned tree, so the full corpus-generation path is not reproducible from the committed snapshot without additional untracked inputs or path reconciliation. Do not import into records.jsonl/gold.tsv or redistribute until Headley/SEALang source rights, dataset license, per-item provenance, target profile and convention are confirmed. Independent bibliographic review (Jenner 1979, DOI 10.15144/PL-C49.431) quotes Headley's target as educated speakers throughout the Khmer-speaking area, not Phnom Penh-specific. It identifies the entries as phonemic transcriptions, notes register is excluded from Headley's vowel-inventory analysis, and critiques convention-specific length/diphthong notation. No verified conversion to the project's typed IPA/register contract exists.
phonemic_convention: The MekongPhon paper calls the seed transcriptions IPA, while Jenner's contemporary review explicitly describes Headley's entries as phonemic transcriptions. Jenner notes that Headley excludes register from the vowel-inventory analysis and discusses idiosyncratic vowel-length/diphthong notation (including length not distinguished for some complex nuclei) and other transcription inconveniences. Treat the source strings as Headley-dictionary phonemic transcription, not as already normalized project IPA; no verified mapping to the project's typed IPA/register contract exists.

title: Incipient tonogenesis in Phnom Penh Khmer: audio recordings, 2011
author: James Kirby
scope: DataShare metadata describes 24-bit/44.1 kHz audio of 16 Phnom Penh Khmer speakers recorded in July 2011, with WAV, segmented Praat TextGrids and Praat Pitch/Formant/PointProcess files. Archive items.zip is 461.93 MB (provider-listed MD5 8688e68e76e8269b8bbf5d19020a230b). Kirby (2014) §§3.1–3.2 reports 20 recruited native Phnom Penh participants (13 female, ages 21–60), a 41-item careful/read task in a carrier sentence (3 randomized repetitions), a separate 15-item colloquial repetition task (3 randomized repetitions), and four participants excluded from subsequent analysis for retaining /r/ in both conditions, leaving 16 analyzed participants. This plausibly explains DataShare's 16-speaker description, but archive folder membership remains unverified.
license: CC BY 4.0
limitations: Not an IPA gold corpus. The DataShare record describes 16 speakers; the paper reports 20 recruited participants, with four excluded from subsequent analysis because they consistently retained /r/ in both conditions (§3.2), leaving 16 analyzed. This plausibly reconciles the count, but archive directory membership is not confirmed. Appendix A lists 41 romanized phonological forms with glosses, not Khmer-script orthography; the paper notes alternate spellings and confirms lexical status with a Khmer assistant. Production task: 41 careful/read self-paced items in the carrier sentence [khñom tha: tiət] at normal rate, 3 randomized repetitions; separate 15-item colloquial repetition task with oral Standard Khmer prompts, 3 repetitions. Neither is standalone isolated citation-form elicitation. The study is focused on /CrV/ variants and does not establish a complete segmental IPA lexicon or balanced series × vowel × coda × prominence matrix. Useful for contextual acoustic review of /r/-loss, F0, aspiration/VOT and voice quality; do not infer a general lexical-tone rule or auto-label /r/. Archive checksum has not been downloaded/verified locally and no token manifest was inspected.
provenance: Edinburgh DataShare full metadata identifies James Kirby, Phnom Penh coverage and July 2011 temporal coverage, states CC BY 4.0, and lists items.zip (461.93 MB; MD5 8688e68e76e8269b8bbf5d19020a230b). Kirby (2014) §§3.1.1–3.2 reports 20 participants, 41 reading items × 3 and 15 colloquial items × 3; four participants who consistently produced /r/ in both conditions were excluded from subsequent analysis. This leaves 16 analyzed participants, plausibly matching the DataShare description, though the archive's actual speaker folders have not been inspected.
contents: WAV audio, segmented Praat TextGrids and Praat Pitch, Formant and PointProcess analysis files.

title: Incipient tonogenesis in Phnom Penh Khmer: supplementary materials, 2011
author: James Kirby

Perceptual CSVs and synthetic KlattGrid stimuli must not be mistaken for natural speech recordings or natural-production measurements. The complete 10-file bundle has not been downloaded or inspected; variable schemas and row-level provenance remain unreviewed. Do not derive a universal tone convention from a bounded /r/-loss experiment.
provenance: Edinburgh DataShare full item metadata identifies James Kirby, Phnom Penh coverage and July–August 2011 temporal coverage, links the files to Kirby (2014), and states CC BY 4.0. The dataset contains anonymised production/perception data, KlattGrid stimulus material, plots and R code. It is separate from the natural audio/TextGrid archive at DOI 10.7488/ds/321.

title: Assessing transcription agreement: Methodological aspects
author: Catia Cucchiarini
scope: Critique of percentage agreement for phonetic transcription: all-or-none symbol matching, chance agreement and missing alignment criteria; proposes alignment and average distance using experimentally derived phonetic feature matrices
limitations: Not a Khmer-specific annotation standard or universal weight matrix; informs reporting and metric design but does not supply validated Khmer feature weights.

title: A Weighted Reliability Measure for Phonetic Transcription
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research 49(6):1391–1411
scope: Weighted reliability measure for phonetic transcription, designed to distinguish degrees of phonetic difference using principles from phonological theory; evaluated with eight coders on speech and vocalisation samples, including three adult languages
limitations: Not a language-specific Khmer feature matrix; the project's current validator does not implement this published measure. A future project metric must not be attributed to Oller and Ramsdell unless their exact algorithm is reproduced.

title: Procesy fonetyczno-fonologiczne w nieregionalnej odmianie języka khmerskiego
author: Piotr Woźnica
scope: Acoustic study of 80 native Khmer speakers from multiple Cambodian regions; examines regional phonetic/phonological variation and argues for a country-wide standard variety
limitations: The thesis warns that the sample is not statistically representative; regional coverage is uneven and the materials are selective/read-text based. It is not a Phnom Penh-only sample or a lexical IPA gold corpus.

title: Khmer ASR Cultural Dataset, Version 3 Part 1

Share-alike obligations and redistribution of any derived IPA must be reviewed before publication.

title: Common Voice Scripted Speech 27.0 — Khmer

title: open-dict-data/ipa-dict — Khmer km.txt

The file is slash-delimited and the upstream README describes its language data as broadly phonemic rather than highly detailed. license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for the third-party Khmer data as identified in the upstream Credits; repository-wide MIT license does not override third-party data terms.

No target dialect/profile, item-level source locators, transcription protocol or per-entry validation evidence is supplied. Preserve all duplicate keys and alternative readings; do not collapse the one divergent duplicate or the 63 multi-pronunciation rows. Broad phonemic transcription is not narrow phonetic gold. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 is non-commercial and share-alike; unsuitable for unrestricted commercial distribution. Keep as an external comparator only unless the project owner approves the licence obligations and the source profile/convention is independently reviewed.

title: Khmer Acoustic Model for Montreal Forced Aligner
scope: Pinned upstream repository main commit 2714994b41ccf875c5b6f6182b48a72f13632dbf. Root README claims a 29,204-entry IPA dictionary, 149,566 audio files/137.01 hours, 1,353,799 word tokens and a pre-trained MFA acoustic model. The root README claims the dictionary data are CC BY-SA 4.0. The separate dictionary/README.md declares CC BY 4.0 for its G2P mapping. The actual repository contains only a six-line dictionary/khmer_ipa_sample.dict; the advertised full dictionary and models/khmer_mfa.zip are absent, as are the 137-hour audio corpus and manual alignment annotations. train_khmer_mfa.ipynb points to a personal Google Drive OpenSLR folder and Khm_full_reduced_dict.txt rather than repository artifacts; align_khmer_audio.ipynb expects external model/dictionary files. The official MontrealCorpusTools/mfa-models registry has no khmer_mfa entry. Root README cites an Interspeech 2026 paper, but the author's XLinCoLab README lists that work as in preparation and the official ISCA Interspeech 2026 archive contains no matching Khmer/Chem entry. dictionary/README.md separately reports 33,091 entries and a 2025 University of Cologne dictionary note. Treat all counts, validation and alignment-performance claims as upstream claims, not independently verified data.
license: Conflicting/incomplete: root README says the acoustic model is MIT and the pronunciation dictionary CC BY-SA 4.0; dictionary/README.md declares CC BY 4.0 for a G2P mapping derived from 33,091 entries; root LICENSE is MIT for software. The actual full dictionary/model artifacts are absent, so no artifact-specific license can be verified. Do not infer that MIT covers the dictionary or speech corpus.
limitations: No full dictionary or model package is available in the pinned repository; only a six-line sample exists. No audio corpus, corpus manifest, per-item provenance, dialect labels, native-review protocol, adjudication records or manual alignment references are present. Dictionary README uses IPA-like but non-standard/ambiguous labels (e.g. digraphs such as /kh/, /th/, /ph/, /ch/, /tɕh/ and inconsistent diphthong notation) and describes unlabelled dialect/register variants. Alignment boundary metrics are not G2P or phonetic-transcription accuracy. Do not import, benchmark or redistribute the sample as a full lexicon; require complete versioned artifacts, hashes, source/rights manifests, target profile and specialist validation.

title: BYU MATRIX Lab Khmer IPA model
scope: 33.6M-parameter BERT encoder-decoder with separate Khmer and IPA tokenizers; model card reports best evaluation loss 0.1736 at checkpoint 26000; the model card's example output is IPA-like. The LREC 2026 MekongPhon paper reports under 2% CER on its own held-out evaluation setup. The associated MekongPhon paper reports 1,314,779 sentence pairs expanded by longest-match lexicon lookup over OPUS from an 8,026-entry seed lexicon; 500 seed entries were reviewed by two proficient L2 speakers, not native annotators.
license: Apache-2.0 as declared by the model card
limitations: The model card license does not resolve rights in the training corpus; MekongPhon repository snapshot has no declared root LICENSE. Source-attested diagnostic results are not independent project gold; model evaluation uses pron_no_tones and does not establish tone/phonation recovery. Published under-2% CER is dictionary-seeded and not independent sentence transcription; reviewer qualifications are L2, not native target-variety adjudicators. The optional benchmark workflow is manual-dispatch only until the MekongPhon corpus license is clarified; the one-time run is retained as historical diagnostic evidence.

title: PhonSobon Khmer G2P (NCKL respelling)
scope: 7.46M-parameter character-level Transformer that predicts NCKL Khmer-script respelling with hyphenated syllable boundaries. The model card reports 83.37% validation word accuracy at epoch 150; this is an upstream validation claim, not a result independently reproduced by this repository.
license: MIT as declared by the model card; this model license does not grant rights to the underlying NCKL-derived training data.
limitations: Output is Khmer-script respelling, not IPA or a typed phonetic result, and must not enter the IPA-first runtime path. The linked dataset derives from the NCKL Khmer Dictionary 2022; its dataset card uses the nckl-khmer-dictionary-2022 license identifier, requests NCKL attribution and says to check NCKL terms before commercial use. No dataset rows or model weights are copied into this repository. No test-set score is stated in the model card.

title: PhonSobon Khmer G2P dataset (derived from NCKL Khmer Dictionary 2022)
scope: 38,629 word-to-pronunciation pairs and 37,755 unique words; published split counts are train 34,770, validation 1,939 and test 1,920. Labels are Khmer-script pronunciation respellings with hyphenated syllable boundaries, not IPA. The dataset card describes a word-level split keeping all readings of a word together.
license: Dataset card identifies nckl-khmer-dictionary-2022; it attributes content to the National Council of Khmer Language (NCKL), Royal Academy of Cambodia, requests NCKL credit and says to check NCKL terms before commercial use. Exact redistribution and derivative-use permissions remain unverified.
limitations: Standard NCKL/Phnom Penh prescribed word pronunciations; not regional or colloquial variants and not running-speech sandhi. This is a respelling/syllabification resource, not a source of IPA labels or an independent phonetic gold set. Do not redistribute or use commercially until NCKL terms are clarified; no rows are imported.

Request the full versioned dictionary/model, checksums, data license, source provenance, and specialist validation before any gold use.

title: Google Language Resources — Khmer TTS lexicon and phonology inventory
scope: Full-file audit of archived Google Language Resources km/data/lexicon.tsv at pinned repository commit a90601024f07ab7e96c911243324e0adeb16da96 (blob d399efeca642b1185786b2982374488c525e37c4; GitHub reports 2.71 MB): 69,415 two-column rows and 69,405 unique spellings (62,175 Khmer-script and 7,230 Latin-script). Ten spelling keys occur twice and each pair has divergent phonemic transcriptions; although the header describes an optional third disambiguating column, every row has only two columns. The lexicon uses 54 distinct phonemic tokens, all present in km/festvox/phonology.json (56 inventory phones: 30 vowels, 24 consonants, 2 silence; sil and pau are unused). The notation is a project-specific phonemic inventory, including ASCII digraphs and doubled-vowel length labels, not a documented strict IPA convention. The companion Festival prompt file km/festvox/txt.done.data (blob 01ca58b32544bcfd44305b91931baf192cce287d) contains 2,748 utterance records across 16 pseudonymous speaker-ID prefixes; it has no gender labels and is not an archive manifest. This is 158 fewer records and one fewer speaker than the paper's 2,906/17 table, so the repository snapshot does not reconcile the published or current OpenSLR archive counts. The 2018 paper reports 70,671 Khmer entries, 1,256 more than the pinned snapshot. It says source words were crawled from Wikipedia/websites, frequency-ranked, manually transcribed by linguists using guidelines and QC'd, but supplies no Khmer-specific guideline, target dialect, per-item source locators, annotator count or error rate.
license: The km/data/lexicon.tsv header explicitly declares CC BY 4.0. The companion km/festvox/phonology.json and km/festvox/txt.done.data have no file-level license header; the repository README says original files are Apache-2.0 unless otherwise noted, while the 2018 paper broadly says all data are CC BY 4.0 unless otherwise noted. Treat the lexicon file as CC BY 4.0; the exact license scope for the companion phonology JSON remains unresolved pending clarification.
limitations: Candidate lexical/phonemic comparator only, not independent IPA gold or an accuracy benchmark. The lexicon includes Khmer-script and Latin-script keys but does not identify target variety; its phonemic convention is not documented as standard IPA and does not encode tone/register. Preserve all ten divergent duplicate spellings as alternatives; the optional disambiguation labels described in the header are absent from the actual two-column rows. The 70,671 paper count differs from the 69,415-row snapshot and requires version clarification. No per-entry source locators or item-level provenance are supplied. The 2,748-row Festival prompt file is not a complete audio manifest and does not identify speaker gender or reconcile the 2,906-file/17-speaker paper table. Do not derive the project’s Phnom Penh careful-citation profile or gold labels from these entries without specialist review and independent annotation.

title: OpenSLR SLR42 — High quality TTS data for Khmer
scope: OpenSLR currently lists one 866 MB archive, km_kh_male.zip, described as male-speaker Khmer speech with audio and a TSV of orthographic transcriptions. The 2018 Sodimana et al. paper reports 17 female speakers, 2,906 audio files and 3:58:00 for Khmer. The pinned Google repository's km/festvox/txt.done.data is a separate Festival prompt index with 2,748 rows and 16 speaker-ID prefixes (no gender labels), also differing from the paper's 2,906 files/17 speakers; it is not a checksum-backed archive manifest. This is a material archive/paper/repository metadata discrepancy requiring manifest-level reconciliation.
license: The current OpenSLR SLR42 page and its linked LICENSE file both declare CC BY-SA 4.0. The 2018 paper reports a general CC BY 4.0 data release unless otherwise noted, so the provider's current archive-specific CC BY-SA declaration takes precedence for the currently listed archive pending clarification of historical versions. The linked license was inspected; the 866 MB archive's internal copy was not downloaded or inspected.
limitations: The corpus contains audio plus Khmer text transcripts, not word-level IPA labels or independent phonetic gold. Do not infer that the currently listed male archive is the same speaker set as the paper's 17-female-speaker table. Obtain and inspect the exact archive manifest, checksum, speaker IDs and license before annotation or derivative use.

title: MekongPhon rule-based Khmer-to-IPA baseline
scope: Experimental rule-based baseline with consonant/register and vowel assignment tables and Khmer tokenization; distinct from the BYU MATRIX neural encoder-decoder. Source code was inspected but not executed by this project.
license: The pinned MekongPhon repository snapshot has no declared root LICENSE. Do not copy or redistribute source code/data pending rights clarification.
limitations: Output conventions, dialect/profile coverage, tokenization behavior and compatibility with the project's typed IPA contract have not been validated. Not an enabled provider, not gold, and not a source of empirical accuracy.

title: The Syllabic and Morphological Structure of Cambodian Words
author: Karnchana Nacaskul
scope: Describes major and minor syllables. For major syllables it reports no final consonant clusters, a listed coda inventory, and no short vowels/short diphthongs in open syllables. It separately defines minor type A (clusters only with /r/ in second position; short /ə/ or /ɔ/; no coda) and type B (single onset; restricted short nucleus; coda among four nasals).
limitations: 1978 description using its own transcription and register analysis. Do not treat minor-type restrictions as global phonotactic bans or assume every coda inventory detail is current for the selected Phnom Penh careful-citation profile. Reconcile with contemporary acoustic/lexical evidence before encoding rules.

title: Khmer Encoding Structure (L2/22-290)
author: Martin Hosken, with Norbert Lindenberg and Makara Sok
scope: Describes modern Khmer orthographic syllable structure as a base plus up to two pre-vowel coengs and an optional dependent vowel; documents coeng use for initial clusters and syllable chaining, and notes that phonetic syllable count can differ from orthographic units. It distinguishes Middle Khmer final coengs from modern dictionary orthography and notes personal-name exceptions.
limitations: This is an encoding/orthography proposal, not a phonological grammar. The two-coeng limit is not a statement that Khmer has at most two onset consonants; chaining can place a previous phonetic coda inside the next orthographic unit.

title: Statistical Khmer Name Romanization
author: Chenchen Ding, Vichet Chea, Masao Utiyama, Eiichiro Sumita, Sethserey Sam, Sopheap Seng
scope: Reports two-consonant onset clusters as common, three as the maximum, and roughly 80 possible consonant combinations. Based on a 7,658-instance Khmer personal-name romanization/alignment study; explicitly discusses mismatch between phonemic syllables and orthographic unbreakable writing units, including silent etymological stacked letters and syllable chaining.
license: The paper states that its manually aligned name-romanization data were released under CC BY-NC-SA for research use; exact current hosting and file-level terms must be checked before reuse.
limitations: A name-romanization/NLP study, not an exhaustive phonological field survey. The approximate 80 cluster types and three-consonant maximum are secondary descriptive claims, not an authoritative exhaustive list or a basis for rejecting individual clusters. No dataset rows are imported.

title: Phonologization of Pitch in Phnom Penh and Standard Khmer for Cluster and Disyllabic Words
author: Sothornin Mam, Pittayawat Pittayaporn, Sireemas Maspong
scope: Compares Standard Khmer and Phnom Penh Khmer using 50 target words, five native speakers (two male, three female), and three repetitions. F0 was measured in the stressed rime. The study reports a lower F0 group for /r>h/ forms and for voiced-onset disyllables in PPK, suggesting that pitch may be phonologizing beyond the previously described /r/-loss context.
limitations: The paper describes the result as possible/incipient phonologization and calls for further study. It is a bounded wordlist and five-speaker sample, not a complete perception study or an independently adjudicated project gold set. Do not add a general Khmer tone rule or infer tone from orthography alone.

title: Cambodian: An Essential Grammar
author: Chhany Sak-Humphry
scope: Publisher preview excerpt discusses CVF and CCVF syllable patterns, short/long nuclei and final consonants. The retrieved excerpt states that short or long vowels are possible when a final is present and that open monosyllables require a long nucleus.
limitations: The retrieved preview excerpt lists /r/ among permitted finals and then also lists /r/ among excluded finals. Do not use this excerpt to settle the coda inventory until the full text or an author/publisher correction resolves the contradiction.

title: Cataloging Service Bulletin No. 43 (Winter 1989), Khmer Romanization
scope: Historical Library of Congress Khmer romanization notes; page 54, Note 10 describes romanization word division using the shortest written form that can stand alone as a word, including Pali and Sanskrit loan-words, while other loan-words retain original-language divisions.
limitations: This is a 1989 policy snapshot, not proof that the same wording remains the current ALA-LC rule. Compare the 1997 ALA-LC table's Note 10 and the 2013 table's Note 8 before implementing a versioned profile.

title: Khmer Romanization Table, 2013 version (ALA-LC)
scope: Current surfaced ALA-LC Khmer cataloguing table; Note 8 says Khmer words are not written separately and any word can be separated when romanizing; Pali/Sanskrit loans follow the same rule, while other loans are divided according to their original language.
limitations: This is a distinct ALA-LC profile, not BGN/PCGN 1972 or Cambodia's national 1995/1997 system. The note does not supply a lexical segmentation algorithm, dictionary, boundary annotations or deterministic treatment of ambiguous compounds.

title: Unicode Technical Note #61: Khmer Encoding Structure, Version 2
author: Martin Hosken
scope: Non-normative technical analysis of Modern Khmer encoding and orthographic-syllable structure, including coengs, consonant shifters, vowel/sign ordering, canonical equivalence, deprecated/discouraged sequences, and shaping. Used only as background for a separately versioned Modern Khmer profile.
license: Unicode Terms of Use apply. Public reproduction, modification, or distribution beyond permitted personal/internal use requires permission unless specifically licensed. This registry records source metadata only and does not reproduce the PDF text or regular expressions.
limitations: Unicode Technical Notes are independently prepared, are not part of the Unicode Standard or a Unicode specification, and do not imply UTC or Unicode Consortium endorsement. The note is an encoding proposal/analysis, not a universal phonological grammar or a replacement for Unicode 18 §16.4. No TN #61-derived grammar is implemented by the current parser; any future use must be a separately versioned profile with independent review. Verify that version 2 remains current before future implementation.

title: Modern Khmer Orthography and Its Dialects
author: Makoto Minegishi
scope: Systematic account of modern Khmer consonant-letter classes, inherent/dependent vowel readings, coda-conditioned vowel values, checked vowels and dialect vowel mergers; distinguishes formal/school pronunciation from colloquial Phnom Penh for specific contrasts.
license: Publisher terms apply; metadata registration only. No text or tables reproduced.
limitations: A systematic partial mapping framework, not a complete formal IPA/G2P algorithm. Orthographic class labels do not consistently describe modern phonetic voicing. Dialect survey is preliminary and includes non-Phnom Penh patterns. Requires combination with current target-profile acoustic evidence and specialist approval.
locators: Sections 1–2, pp. 43–53 (series and vowel-sign rules, coda conditioning, checked vowels); Section 3, pp. 55–66 (dialect survey and vowel mergers).

title: Acoustic transitions in Khmer word-initial clusters: audio recordings, 2013
author: James Kirby
related_study: Kirby, James. 2014. Acoustic transitions in Khmer word-initial clusters. Proceedings of the 10th International Seminar on Speech Production, pp. 230–233.
scope: 24-bit/44.1 kHz audio recorded in Phnom Penh in January 2013 from 10 native Phnom Penh Khmer speakers (3 female): 79 lexical items, 3 repetitions per item, two self-selected speech-rate conditions. Each subject directory contains WAV and segmented Praat TextGrid files. Filename pattern is subject-rate-Khmer-orthography-repetition (e.g. s1-fast-កណ្ដាល-1). The 2014 paper analyses 61 items containing 35 onset-cluster types, plus eight CəC/CəN comparison monosyllables; the first block was instructed slowly and carefully, the second as rapidly as possible, and tokens were embedded in /kñom tha: tiət/ ‘I say again’.
license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), stated in the repository's DataShare item metadata and license bundle.
contents: WAV audio and associated segmented Praat TextGrids; no IPA annotations are supplied.
provenance: DataShare item metadata identifies James Kirby as creator, University of Edinburgh as publisher, recording location Phnom Penh, Cambodia, and recording date January 2013. The full item metadata identifies CC BY 4.0. The paper's Methods §2.1 (PDF pp. 1–2) specifies 10 native Phnom Penh Khmer speakers, 79 lexical items, three repetitions, two speech-rate conditions, the slow-and-careful instruction for the first block, frame sentence, and 61 analysed cluster items.
status_scope: Candidate source for direct phonetic review and exact external audio/TextGrid locators; not a project IPA label source and not a complete citation-form lexical benchmark.
limitations: The task is a controlled reading experiment in a carrier sentence, not a standalone citation-form elicitation. The slow condition is described as slowly and carefully but is not automatically equivalent to the project's careful-citation profile. The paper focuses on onset clusters and eight short-vowel comparison words; it does not establish coverage of the full series × vowel × coda × stress space. TextGrids are segmentation/measurement aids, not independent IPA transcriptions. Item-level Khmer orthography is present in archive filenames, but the complete 79-item list has not yet been enumerated or manually audited from the archive. Do not select pilot items until the archive is inspected, target-profile fit is reviewed, and each exact token locator is recorded. Attribute source and dataset under CC BY 4.0; preserve source attribution and license notices for any permitted reuse. No archive was downloaded or imported in this audit.

title: Phonological Principles for Automatic Phonetic Transcription of Khmer Orthographic Words
author: Makara Sok; Larin Adams
scope: PACLIC 30, pp. 417–424. Describes a Thrax-based two-stage Khmer orthography-to-pronunciation system: orthographic forms to phonemic forms intended to represent careful speech, then phonemic forms to close phonetic forms intended to approximate rapid/ordinary colloquial speech. Reports series assimilation, vowel modification, orthographic syllable grouping and sound-change rules. Uses a 140-word hand-selected validation set, a 1967 Chuon Nath dictionary corpus and Headley (1997) phonemic transcriptions.
rights_basis: The PACLIC 30 proceedings front matter states that copyright of contributed papers is reserved by the respective authors and gives a general all-rights-reserved notice. No explicit open license for this contribution was verified.
limitations: Not an independent benchmark or project gold; not an IPA gold corpus. The 140-word set is hand-selected and its expected phonemic forms are taken from Headley (1997), with phonetic forms manually produced by the authors; it is not described as blinded, independently double-annotated or adjudicated. The 10,110-word experiment uses a dictionary-derived dataset and Headley phonemic transcriptions rather than an independent recorded-speech reference; the paper does not provide a reproducible item-level split, full gold labels, IAA or a target dialect/profile matching khmer-pph-careful-citation-v1. It explicitly excludes Pali/Sanskrit loans at this stage and ignores 999 compound words outside its syllable groupings. The second stage models rapid/colloquial phonetic reduction, not the project's careful citation target. Several table/OCR-extracted IPA/ASCII values appear inconsistent or garbled; do not copy the tables into runtime mappings without source-page visual verification and specialist review. The paper's reported 97.86% and 98.43% figures are author-reported results for its own grammar/data, not transferable accuracy claims.
provenance: Primary full text: ACL Anthology Y16-3013, PACLIC 30, pp. 417–424. Sections 4–5 describe Chuon Nath (1967) dictionary cleanup and character mapping; §6 and Tables 5–6 describe series assimilation and vowel modification; §7 separates phonemic-to-phonetic rapid-speech rules; §8 reports author-run evaluation. The proceedings front matter, p. ii, reserves contributed-paper copyright to the respective authors.
evidence_locators: pp. 417–418 §§1–4 (orthography, data preparation and 140-word validation); pp. 419–421 §§5–6 (mapping, series assimilation, monosyllables/disyllables, Bantoc); p. 422 §§6.4–7 (sound changes and rapid-speech phonetic layer); p. 423 §8 (reported results); proceedings front matter p. ii (rights).

title: Google Khmer pronunciation lexicon and FineWeb-2 frequency dictionary
scope: 61,980 normalized Khmer word/count entries are used for provisional frequency-weighted segmentation. The complete Google source TSV is bundled with its original phonemic column for provenance; the compact runtime JSON excludes phonemic strings. The historical 3,009-entry sample remains as a regression baseline and all of its words/counts are preserved in the full table. The separate 209,330-row bigram table is generated as a research artifact but is not currently used by the runtime.
limitations: No independent manually adjudicated Khmer segmentation gold corpus has been evaluated; segmentation accuracy remains NOT ASSESSED. A larger dictionary increases lexical coverage but does not prove boundary correctness. FineWeb counts are web-text frequencies, not pronunciation or dialect evidence. Google phonemic strings are not project IPA and are not fed to the Ukrainian IPA adapter.
